t: My boss wants me to change the figures
s: I work in finance at an electronic components firm. Just before quarter-end, the general manager told me to book an unconfirmed order as revenue now: “It’s only early. We’ll balance it next quarter, and the bank needs this quarter’s numbers for our loan.” He said it lightly, but I know this report goes to the bank and our shareholders.
j: In the wilderness Jesus refused Satan’s shortcut. He chose the Father’s way rather than grabbing the kingdom first and sorting it out later. His yes was yes and his no was no. Jesus would tell the truth gently and would not let fear make the decision.

b.p: The numbers on a report are today’s scales and weights. God cares not only that the result looks good but that the measuring is honest. Massaged accounts are “a false balance”, even if it is only ‘for now’.
b.t: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but accurate weights are his delight.

h: Lord, I admit I’m afraid of losing my job and of being seen as difficult. Help me see the real weight of this step, and give me a calm heart and the right words, so that fear no longer leads me.
g: Changing the figures might protect my boss’s face and my position for a while, but the glory goes to the self that wants to be in charge. Holding to honesty is letting Jesus be King in the finance office.
x: The bank, the shareholders, colleagues, even my boss could all be harmed by false figures; if it comes out, everyone in the company suffers. When I decline, I can protect his dignity by speaking privately, not confronting him in front of others.
n: Explain the revenue recognition rules and the risks to the general manager privately, and offer an alternative, such as a note disclosing orders in progress. Keep a written record. If pressured, consult an accountant or legal professional, remembering that we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

t: Padding expenses: everyone does it
s: I’m in sales at a multinational and travel a lot. The unspoken rule in my department is to round up taxi receipts and claim private dinners as client meals. My manager says, “The travel allowance is too low anyway; everyone does it.” When I claim honestly, my totals are clearly lower, and colleagues feel I’m spoiling it for them.
j: Jesus never drifted along because ‘everyone does it’, yet he didn’t look down on people either. He went into Zacchaeus’ house, and grace moved that tax collector to repay what he had taken. Jesus would live honestly and be gentle with colleagues who haven’t changed yet.

b.p: An expense claim is “a very little”, yet it tests character. Faithfulness on one receipt trains a life that can later be trusted with much; small dishonesties slowly rewrite our conscience.
b.t: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.

h: Holy Spirit, show me: am I more afraid of being left out, or of grieving you? As I claim honestly, keep me from judging others, give me peace, and stop me feeling superior.
g: A few extra pounds claimed gives glory to greed and group pressure. An honest claim lets Jesus be glorified on an ordinary slip of paper and shows the company that Christians can be trusted.
x: Honest claims may make colleagues feel compared. I needn’t make a stand or report anyone; I just keep my own receipts straight. If asked, I can say, “I just want to sleep well,” keeping the relationship and refusing to be the office police.
n: Start with the next receipt and fill it in truthfully. If the allowance really is unfair, raise it formally with your manager and ask the company to review it, meeting a genuine need through proper channels rather than plugging the gap in grey ways.

t: A supplier’s red envelope
s: I handle procurement for a construction company. Before the New Year, a long-standing building supplier handed me a thick red envelope: “Just a token. Look after us in future tenders.” Their quality is fine and their prices slightly high. Colleagues say gifts like this are normal in the trade, and refusing makes you look awkward.
j: Jesus could not be bought, and he was not afraid of offending the powerful. He ate with tax collectors without joining their ways; he loved people, but never let favours sway his judgement. Jesus would decline the ‘token’ and still keep the friendship with the supplier.

b.p: The worst thing about a bribe is not the amount but that it “blinds those who have sight”. Once accepted, my judgement of that supplier is no longer free. God wants us to keep our eyes clear.
b.t: You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds those who have sight and perverts the words of the righteous.

h: Lord, I admit that envelope tempted me, and I’m afraid things will become strained. Give me wise words, so that I can refuse without shaming anyone and stay clear about where the line is.
g: Taking the envelope gives glory to self-interest and favours. Declining it shows both company and supplier that at this purchasing desk Jesus is King, not the red envelope.
x: The supplier may lose face, and other bidders could be treated unfairly. When I decline, I can first thank him for the kindness, then explain company policy and my wish for a long partnership, giving him a graceful way out.
n: Return it unopened as soon as possible and report it to your manager or compliance team as policy requires, keeping a record. Then assess this supplier by the same standard as everyone else: no punishment for the refusal and no favours for the friendship.

t: Asked to hide a product defect
s: I’m in quality control at a food factory. Sampling found faulty seals on a batch, which could affect its shelf life. The plant manager said, “The odds are low and reworking it costs too much. Ship it, and we’ll deal with complaints if they come.” Next week this batch goes onto the shelves of dozens of supermarkets.
j: Jesus valued the smallest and least noticed. He spoke the truth and cared for people’s lives. He would never trade other people’s health for sales; he would put the facts on the table clearly and courageously, and help find a responsible way forward.

b.p: Hiding a defect is a kind of lie. Paul says to speak truth with our neighbour, “for we are members of one another”. Customers, company and I are bound together; deceiving others ends up wounding ourselves too.
b.t: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbour, for we are members of one another.

h: Holy Spirit, keep me from being cowed by the manager’s tone or losing my temper. Help me picture the families who will buy this batch, and give me courage to say what must be said.
g: Shipping it protects this quarter’s figures and pride. Facing the defect honestly lets Jesus be glorified and builds a brand that customers can trust.
x: Consumers’ health is most at risk, and the manager and line staff fear being blamed. Focus on solving the problem, not on whose fault it is, so that everyone works together to keep the losses down.
n: Put the test data into a written report and explain the risks and options (rework, batch screening) to the plant manager and senior management. If you are asked to conceal a food safety issue, use the company’s internal reporting channels and seek professional advice if needed.

t: Tempted to copy someone else’s design
s: I’m a designer at an advertising agency, and the client wants to see the pitch tomorrow morning. Online I found an overseas designer’s work that is exactly the right style; I’d only need to change the colours and fonts. My manager says, “The client won’t notice. Just get it through.” I’ve worked late three nights running.
j: Jesus never proved himself by taking someone else’s credit; he gave the glory to the Father. When he was weary, he withdrew to pray rather than taking a shortcut. Jesus would honour that designer’s hard work and be honest that he had run out of time.

b.p: Copying is the way of one who “perverts his ways”. It may get through tonight but plants a mine that will “be found out”. The upright road looks slower, yet it is the one where we walk surely, with our craft and conscience intact.
b.t: He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.

h: Lord, I’m exhausted and frightened of having nothing to show. Quieten me, show me my real gifts and limits, and give me enough ideas and strength for tonight.
g: A copied design gives me a moment’s credit but steals someone else’s glory. Handing in my own work, imperfect as it may be, lets Jesus be glorified.
x: The original designer’s rights, the client’s brand and the agency’s reputation could all be harmed. If time is genuinely short, honesty protects trust with my manager and client far better than secret copying.
n: Use the reference as inspiration only and develop your own idea. Tell your manager honestly where things stand and suggest presenting a direction first, with the final design later. If copyright is a concern, ask the company’s legal team or a professional.

t: Doing personal things on work time
s: I’m an administrator in a government office, and the workload is light. Many colleagues stream dramas, shop online or run side businesses during work hours; some slip out to collect children and ask others to swipe their cards. I’m on my phone more and more, and I’ve even thought of asking someone to clock in for me.
j: Jesus was known as a carpenter (Mark 6:3); we can imagine him working wholeheartedly on days no one was watching. Unseen, he was still faithful to what the Father entrusted to him. Jesus would treat working hours as time placed in his hands by the Father.

b.p: This verse changes the question of whom we work for. Even with no manager watching and no KPI, we work “heartily, as for the Lord”. Office hours are paid by the employer, but entrusted by God.
b.t: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.

h: Lord, help me notice: am I bored, tired, or have I lost the meaning of my work? Rekindle my heart for it, and make me faithful in this small place.
g: Slacking and fake clock-ins let ‘my comfort’ be king. Working from the heart makes even one corner of the office a place where Jesus is glorified.
x: Clocking in for others drags in the colleague who helps and leaves hardworking staff to carry the load. I needn’t criticise anyone; I can simply stop. If asked to swipe for someone, I can kindly decline and say I don’t want either of us at risk.
n: List the tasks you could take on each day, and use quiet times to learn new skills or help colleagues. Decline requests to clock in for others. If you are under-used for long, tell your manager you are willing to take on more.

t: Should I polish my CV a little?
s: I’m thirty-five, have managed restaurants for ten years, and want to move into operations at a large chain. A friend suggested calling myself ‘Regional Operations Manager’ instead of ‘Restaurant Manager’ and listing an unfinished course as a qualification: “HR only scans for keywords; everyone dresses it up.” I really need this job.
j: Jesus never needed to inflate who he was. His worth came from the Father’s approval, not a title. He was honest about who he was and willing to be misunderstood. Jesus would present his real experience clearly and powerfully, without making anything up.

b.p: Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but “those who do the truth are his delight”. Honesty isn’t underselling yourself: presenting ten years of experience truthfully and well is the presentation that pleases God.
b.t: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

h: Lord, I’m afraid my experience isn’t good enough. Remind me that my worth is in your hands, not on my CV. Show me the work you have already done in me, and help me describe it honestly.
g: An inflated CV makes me look better and keeps the glory for myself. An honest CV lets God be the provider of my work, and he receives the glory.
x: Exaggerated credentials set false expectations for a future manager and team; when discovered, they damage trust and my reputation. Only honesty builds working relationships that last.
n: Translate your experience into concrete results (team size, revenue growth, new branches) and let true figures speak. Describe the unfinished course as ‘in progress’. Ask a trusted friend in the industry or a careers adviser to look over your CV.

t: Fake policies to hit my target
s: I’m a sales supervisor at an insurance company, just short of the year-end ranking that wins an overseas trip. A colleague showed me how to write a few policies in relatives’ names and cancel them once the ranking closes: “Nothing in the rules says you can’t.” My team are excited about the trip too.
j: Facing temptation, Jesus would rather go without all the kingdoms of the world than bow to what is wrong. He didn’t prove himself by putting on a show; he trusted the Father to provide in due time. Jesus would give up the prize and choose faithfulness where no one sees.

b.p: “Better is a little with righteousness, than great revenues with injustice.” Prizes and rankings pass; God looks at how we gain them. The ‘little’ won with integrity is really much.
b.t: Better is a little with righteousness, than great revenues with injustice.

h: Holy Spirit, show me what this ‘loophole’ really is and stop me deceiving myself. Give me courage to explain to my team, and peace even in the disappointment of losing the prize.
g: Fake policies bring a moment of glory to me and my team, and the glory goes to the ranking. Facing my real figures honestly lets Jesus be King even in a sales contest.
x: Relatives whose names are used, genuine clients and the company’s auditors could all be caught up in it, and the team may learn to cut corners. Explain your reasons honestly to the team, then set a legitimate next goal together.
n: Refuse to write fake policies and push honestly through the last weeks. Tell the team your decision and why, and find other ways to reward them. If the rules are unclear, check with the compliance department.

t: My manager took credit for my work
s: I’m an engineer at a tech company. I spent two months optimising our systems and cut server costs by a third. At the quarterly meeting my manager presented the result to senior leaders, said only “our department”, and hinted it was his idea. Colleagues are indignant on my behalf, and I feel angry and hurt.
j: Jesus did many miracles and often told people not to spread the news; he didn’t need applause to know his worth. Yet he was no doormat, and when the time was right he made the truth plain. Jesus would first bring his hurt to the Father, then deal with it calmly.

b.p: Humility means placing ourselves “under the mighty hand of God”, trusting that he will “exalt you in due time”, not my manager’s slides. This isn’t a call to permanent silence, but freedom from needing to grab back credit to prove myself.
b.t: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.

h: Lord, I really am hurt, and I want justice. Heal my heart first, and help me discern: is this a fact that needs stating, or my self-centred wish to be seen?
g: Fighting to reclaim credit may bring glory to me. Letting go of the score and explaining gently at the right time lets Jesus be glorified in the hurt.
x: My relationship with my manager and the team’s mood could both suffer from a moment’s anger. A private word protects the relationship better than a public row, and when colleagues take my side, I shouldn’t join in criticising him.
n: Speak to your manager privately. Begin with thanks, describe your contribution specifically, and ask how the team’s individual roles might be made visible to senior leaders in future. Keep work logs and weekly reports so your results are seen naturally.

t: My boss humiliates me in front of everyone
s: I’m a sous-chef. The head chef has a terrible temper: when service slows he slams pans and calls me “brainless” and “useless” in front of everyone. I need this experience, but my stomach churns before every shift and I replay his words all evening at home.
j: When Jesus was insulted, he didn’t insult back, but neither did he accept those words as true; he entrusted himself to the Father who judges justly. He knew who he was, so humiliation didn’t define him. Jesus would keep his dignity and, when needed, leave an unreasonable situation.

b.p: Not answering back isn’t bottling it up but entrusting: handing justice and my identity to God, who “judges righteously”. This verse doesn’t tell us to endure everything; it keeps hatred and self-loathing from ruling our hearts.
b.t: When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didnt threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.

h: Lord, those words keep ringing in my ears. Replace them with your words and remind me that I am loved by you. Show me when to speak and when to leave.
g: Hitting back gives the glory to anger; quietly putting myself down lets the lie win. Standing secure in who I am before God and responding sensibly lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My own body and mind are being hurt, and other kitchen staff may be too. Caring for myself is not selfish. If others suffer the same, we can support one another and look for proper channels together.
n: When the chef is calm, tell him privately that you will work on your speed but ask him to stop the personal insults. Note dates and what was said. If it continues or affects your health, raise it with senior management or HR, and seek help from someone you trust or a professional counsellor.

t: My manager wants me to take the blame
s: I’m a project assistant at a logistics company. A major client’s shipment was a week late because my manager forgot to check the customs documents. Before the review meeting he told me privately, “You’re junior; take the hit. I’ll look after you.” I’m afraid life will be hard if I refuse.
j: Jesus bore our sins out of willing love, not because someone forced him to lie. He never gave false testimony to please anyone. Jesus would refuse a false confession and still not rush to shame anyone publicly.

b.p: Truth and love come together. Not admitting a fault that isn’t mine is truthful; not exposing my manager in public is loving. Both together are the maturity of growing up “into him who is the head, Christ”.
b.t: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.

h: Lord, I’m afraid of losing my manager’s favour and of seeming disloyal. Give me courage and gentle words, so that I neither lie nor take revenge.
g: Taking the blame might earn me a favour, but it gives glory to a lie. Speaking the truth in love lets Jesus be King in that review meeting.
x: My manager fears the consequences; the client and company need the real cause to improve the process; I must also protect my own name. I can focus on the gap in the process rather than naming names.
n: Reply to your manager privately: you will gladly help put it right, but you cannot admit to an error you didn’t make. In the meeting, focus on improving the process, such as a double-check list. If pressured, keep a record and, if needed, ask a more senior manager or HR for help.

t: My boss told me to break the law
s: I’m the environmental and safety officer at a small chemical plant. My boss told me to discharge a batch of waste liquid into the nearby stream at night. Disposal is too expensive, he said: “If we’re caught, the fine is cheaper.” Mine is the only income in our family, and this job was hard to find.
j: Jesus obeyed the Father to the end but never obeyed sin. He respected those in authority, but when human commands clashed with God’s will he chose God. Jesus would say a clear ‘no’ and would care about the people living downstream.

b.p: Scripture teaches us to respect authority, but obedience has limits. When an order would make us sin and harm others, “We must obey God rather than men.” That is a boundary, not rebellion.
b.t: But Peter and the apostles answered, We must obey God rather than men.

h: Lord, I’m frightened of losing our income. Help me trust that you are my provider. Give me courage to refuse and wisdom to protect myself and my family.
g: Dumping the waste lets profit and fear be king. Refusing to break the law lets Jesus be glorified in the factory and shows that God cares for the world he made.
x: Residents, farmers and wildlife downstream would all be harmed, and my boss could later face far worse consequences. My family needs a steady income, so I must act carefully, not rashly.
n: Refuse clearly and propose a legal disposal plan with a cost comparison. Keep a record of the instruction. You may consult a lawyer or the relevant authority about your rights and how to report it. Meanwhile, pray and plan with your family and trusted people at church.

t: An impossible deadline
s: I’m an auditor at an accounting firm. In busy season my manager gave me three clients at once and wants all done in a week, when one normally takes a week. I already work until midnight every day, and he just says, “Young people should be able to take it.” I daren’t refuse in case I look lazy.
j: Jesus knew his mission and knew human limits; however large the crowds, he withdrew to pray. He wasn’t driven by others’ expectations but kept the Father’s rhythm. Jesus would be honest about what could and couldn’t be done.

b.p: Jethro told Moses, “the thing is too heavy for you.” That is God-given wisdom: admitting our limits isn’t weakness but responsibility to the work and to people. Overload only means we “wear away”, and others with us.
b.t: Moses father-in-law said to him, The thing that you do is not good. You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.

h: Lord, I’m afraid of letting people down. Show me that my worth isn’t in how much I carry but in faithfulness. Give me courage to say how things really are.
g: Pushing myself until I collapse lets ‘I must be approved’ be king. Talking honestly about the workload lets Jesus be glorified in my limits.
x: My health, my family and the quality of the audits could all suffer, and clients need accurate reports. When I speak to my manager, I can stand on our shared goal of doing the work well.
n: List the hours each engagement needs and their priorities, and ask your manager to help decide the order or bring in more people. If long-term overwork is affecting your health, seek help from someone you trust, a doctor or another professional.

t: Asked to spy on a colleague
s: I’m a team leader on a department store counter. The area manager privately asked me to report a senior colleague’s every move each day: when she takes breaks, what she says to customers, whether she slacks. “She may be transferred; we need evidence.” She has always been kind to me and taught me a great deal.
j: Jesus didn’t scheme behind people’s backs; he spoke openly. He respected rightful authority but took no part in hidden traps. Jesus would know the difference between honest work reporting and deliberately collecting ammunition.

b.p: A gossip “betrays a confidence”, while a trustworthy person keeps it. This isn’t about covering wrongdoing; it is about refusing to become a tool for prying into and spreading other people’s private affairs.
b.t: One who brings gossip betrays a confidence, but one who is of a trustworthy spirit is one who keeps a secret.

h: Lord, show me my motives: am I afraid of the manager, or keen to impress? Help me find your way between respecting my superior and treating my colleague well.
g: Secret surveillance to please a superior gives glory to power and fear. Handling it openly lets Jesus be King at the counter.
x: My senior colleague could be wronged by one-sided reports, and our relationship and the trust on the counter would suffer. Management needs facts, but they should be gathered openly and fairly.
n: Tell the area manager you will report honestly on work matters such as sales and rotas, but it isn’t appropriate to record a colleague’s every move in secret; suggest he speaks to her directly, and if there are real problems, uses the formal appraisal process.

t: My manager makes me uncomfortable
s: I’m new at an architecture practice. When we work late, my manager sits very close, tells me I “look lovely”, and has messaged inviting me to dinner alone at the weekend “to talk about promotion”. I said no once, and since then he ignores me in meetings. I don’t know if I’m oversensitive or if something is really wrong.
j: When Joseph was propositioned, he didn’t linger or argue; he left at once. Jesus respects every person’s body and dignity and never looks down on the oppressed. Jesus would protect himself and have the courage to tell the truth.

b.p: Joseph “ran outside”. Some situations are not for gritting our teeth but for leaving quickly. Guarding our boundaries is in line with God’s heart; it is neither rude nor disobedient.
b.t: She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.

h: Lord, my heart is in turmoil and I doubt myself. Help me know this is not my fault, and give me clear judgement and courage to protect myself.
g: Silent endurance lets someone keep abusing his power. Setting boundaries and seeking help lets God’s justice and protection be glorified.
x: My safety and wellbeing need care first, and other colleagues may be going through the same. Speaking up may protect them too.
n: Avoid being alone with him and decline private invitations clearly and politely. Keep messages and a record of incidents, and tell someone you trust. Use the company’s harassment procedure or HR, and seek professional counselling or legal advice if needed.

t: My new manager knows less than I do
s: I’m a senior nurse at a hospital. The new ward manager came from an administrative post with little clinical experience, and her rotas and decisions often seem unprofessional to me. Junior nurses quietly come to me for advice, and I’ve realised I’m coaching them on how to get round her instructions.
j: David had the chance to kill Saul but would not lift his hand against “the LORD’s anointed”. Jesus, wiser than anyone, also honoured the order the Father had set. Jesus would use his expertise to support the team, not build a rival camp.

b.p: David respected Saul’s position not because Saul was doing well, but out of reverence for the order God had set. Even when a superior falls short, we do not undermine them or “stretch out my hand against him”.
b.t: He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORDs anointed.”

h: Lord, I admit there is pride in me; I think I’m better than she is. Bring me back to my rightful place, to serve her with my experience rather than replace her.
g: Leading juniors round the ward manager gives glory to my expertise and influence. Humble support and fitting advice let Jesus be King on the ward.
x: The ward manager needs time to settle; the juniors are caught in the middle; patient safety matters most of all. Honest advice in private cares for everyone better than dividing the team behind her back.
n: Arrange to meet the ward manager, share your clinical observations and suggestions, and offer to help her get to know the ward. Stop leading others round her instructions. Where patient safety is at stake, raise it through proper channels.

t: The free rider on our team
s: I’m an analyst at a consultancy. There are four of us on a project. One colleague has plenty of opinions in meetings but rarely delivers any analysis, and then rushes to present at the end. Our manager only sees the final result, and I feel I’m being used as free labour.
j: Jesus worked alongside his disciples. He saw who was working and who was dodging, yet he didn’t grow bitter. He named problems honestly and gave people the chance to change. Jesus would do his own part and wisely let responsibility return to the one who should carry it.

b.p: “Let each man examine his own work”: first, have I done my part? “Each man will bear his own burden”: let others carry what is theirs. No need to compare, and no need to carry everyone.
b.t: But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else. For each man will bear his own burden.

h: Lord, I’m resentful. Stop me comparing, and give me wisdom to make the division of work clear in a gentle way.
g: Complaining and freezing him out lets bitterness rule. Clear roles and doing my part willingly let Jesus be glorified in teamwork.
x: This colleague may be struggling with ability or with something at home, and resentment could crack the team’s spirit. Ask privately first, then talk about roles, protecting his dignity.
n: At the next meeting, suggest a simple table of tasks and deadlines so that everyone’s responsibilities are visible. Ask your colleague privately whether he is facing difficulties. If nothing changes, explain the actual division of work to your manager.

t: The office gossip group
s: I’m a sales assistant at a trading company. Colleagues set up a LINE group where every day they discuss our manager’s private life and new staff’s clothes, and share screenshots. I haven’t left, and sometimes I can’t resist a laughing emoji. Lately they’ve been speculating whether a colleague on long leave has “something going on”.
j: When the crowd surrounded the woman caught in adultery, Jesus didn’t join in the accusations; he turned each person back to examine themselves. His words were full of grace. Jesus wouldn’t talk about people behind their backs, but he would care for the one being talked about.

b.p: To judge whether to say something, ask: does it build others up? Will it “give grace to those who hear”? Gossip brings a moment of closeness but quietly tears people down. God wants our mouths to be tools for building.
b.t: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

h: Holy Spirit, remind me in the moment before I tap reply. Show me how to stay out of the talk without judging my colleagues.
g: Gossip gives glory to the in-group’s sense of superiority. Refusing to pass things on and speaking words that build lets Jesus be glorified even in a small chat group.
x: Those being discussed are the ones most easily hurt, including the colleague on leave. I needn’t shame anyone in the group; quietly changing the subject or gradually stepping back keeps relationships better than public rebuke.
n: Stop responding to gossip and steer the conversation to work or something positive. If it crosses a line, say gently, “Let’s not guess.” Contact the colleague on leave privately with a sincere greeting and blessing.

t: A close friend resents my promotion
s: I work at a bank branch. A friend who joined when I did and I both applied for assistant manager, and I got it. Since then she no longer invites me to lunch and coldly contradicts me in meetings. I treasure our friendship but don’t know what to do; I’ve even thought of giving the post up.
j: Jesus wasn’t afraid of being misunderstood, but he took the initiative in love. When his disciples argued about who was greatest, he answered with a servant’s posture. Jesus would be humble, neither flaunting nor hiding, and show his friend by actions that he still cared.

b.p: She may well be weeping inside: disappointed, embarrassed, worried about her future. To “weep with those who weep” is to understand her feelings first, not to expect her to rejoice for me straight away.
b.t: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

h: Lord, help me see her sorrow, not just her coldness towards me. May this promotion be not a reason for pride but an opportunity to serve.
g: Flaunting it or freezing her out gives glory to self-centredness. Staying humble and loving in promotion lets Jesus be glorified in our working relationships.
x: My friend is grieving a loss, I’m hurting too, and the branch is watching us. There’s no need to rush the repair; give each other time and space, treat her fairly, and neither fawn nor withdraw.
n: Find a relaxed moment to invite her for coffee, say sincerely that you value the friendship and understand her disappointment. At work, share opportunities fairly and give her room to shine. Repair takes time; keep praying for her.

t: A shouting match in a meeting
s: I lead the programming team at a games company. In a product meeting the art lead said publicly that our code was “so bad it’s dragging the schedule”. I snapped back that his designs were “impossible to build”. We got louder and louder until the meeting broke up. Now everyone is waiting to see how it ends.
j: When people challenged Jesus, he sometimes stayed silent and sometimes answered gently, but he never let anger take over. He also taught us to go and be reconciled. Jesus would deal with his own heart first, then go to the other person.

b.p: Conflict isn’t for group chats or gossip; it is for a face-to-face talk “between you and him alone”. The aim isn’t to win but to have “gained back your brother”, valuing the relationship above the argument.
b.t: If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.

h: Lord, I’m still angry and I think I’m right. Show me my share of the blame and give me the humility to be the first to make peace.
g: Insisting he apologises first gives glory to pride. Making peace and solving the problem together lets Jesus be glorified in the project.
x: Both teams could be dragged in, and the product schedule will suffer. In private, apologise first for your tone, then discuss the technical issues, protecting each other’s dignity.
n: Find the art lead today and apologise privately for your tone in the meeting, then book a time to work through the technical limits and design needs together. If needed, ask the producer to mediate and agree a way of communicating that suits you both.

t: Bullied by senior colleagues
s: I’m a newly qualified teacher at a state school. Several senior teachers make sarcastic remarks about my teaching in the staffroom, push the hardest classes and the chores onto me, and have told parents I’m “not up to the job”. I often cry while marking at night and have started to dread walking into the staffroom.
j: Jesus was shunned and falsely accused. He didn’t repay evil with evil, but he didn’t pretend all was well either; when necessary he avoided danger and exposed hypocrisy. Jesus would stand firm in the Father’s love and wisely protect himself.

b.p: “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you”: peace is my direction, but it isn’t wholly in my hands. When someone keeps causing harm, setting boundaries and seeking help does not contradict the call to peace.
b.t: If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

h: Lord, I’m tired and afraid. Hold me close and remind me that your love doesn’t change with what others say. Give me a clear head to know my next step.
g: Repaying evil with evil gives glory to hatred. Staying good in suffering and bravely seeking justice lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wellbeing needs care first, and pupils and parents may also be affected by the rumours. Caring for people includes caring for myself; I don’t have to bear this alone.
n: Record the date and details of each incident and report them to a trusted head of department, the head teacher or the school’s grievance procedure. Find someone you trust to walk with you, and seek counselling or other professional support if needed. Keep teaching well and let the facts speak.

t: Left out by colleagues at lunch
s: I’ve just transferred from Taipei to our Singapore office. Local colleagues chat in Hokkien mixed with English and go to lunch in a group every day, but never invite me. In meetings my ideas are often passed over. I eat lunch alone every day and feel invisible.
j: Jesus often went to people on the margins: the Samaritan woman at the well, Zacchaeus up the tree. He was also rejected in his home town. Jesus knows what loneliness feels like, and he would reach out first rather than wait to be accepted.

b.p: In an unfamiliar place, God’s promise is “I am with you”. My worth doesn’t depend on being invited. God will strengthen and help me and, in his time, open the way.
b.t: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Dont be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.

h: Lord, I feel so alone. Let me sense your presence, and give me courage to take one small step towards the people around me.
g: Self-pity or hostility lets bitterness rule. Blessing others even in loneliness lets Jesus be glorified far from home.
x: My colleagues may not be excluding me on purpose; their habits and culture are simply different. I also need to look after my feelings so that loneliness doesn’t harden into prejudice against the whole team.
n: Ask a friendly-looking colleague to recommend a place nearby, or invite them to lunch. Learn a few local phrases. Join a local church or small group to build support outside work.

t: I found a colleague’s records falsified
s: I’m a research assistant at a pharmaceutical company. I noticed gaps in the data records of the colleague at the next bench; some entries were filled in afterwards, which could affect the results. He is his family’s breadwinner and under great strain, as his wife has been ill. I’m afraid that reporting it will cost him his job.
j: Jesus never turned a blind eye to wrongdoing, nor was he quick to condemn; he spoke privately first and restored gently. Jesus would care about truthful data and about this colleague’s situation.

b.p: Faced with someone else’s fault, we are to “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”: neither ignoring it nor kicking someone when they are down, and “looking to yourself”, without any sense of superiority.
b.t: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also arent tempted.

h: Lord, help me approach him with gentleness, not judgement. Help me also discern when those above us must be told.
g: Covering up gives glory to favours; exposing him and enjoying the drama gives glory to self-righteousness. Gentle restoration with integrity lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My colleague and his family, future patients using the medicine and the whole research team are all affected. Speaking privately first and giving him the chance to correct it cares for both the person and the truth.
n: Speak to him privately with concern, explain what you saw and encourage him to correct it with your manager himself. If he refuses and the issue affects the reliability of the research and patient safety, you must report it as procedures require, while continuing to care for him.

t: A new colleague keeps asking me questions
s: I’m a senior customer service agent at an e-commerce company. A new colleague is slow to learn and asks me the same questions twenty times a day, so my own work keeps slipping. My manager says, “You’re experienced; help her out,” but hasn’t reduced my workload. I’ve grown impatient and my tone has become sharp.
j: Jesus taught disciples who often didn’t understand, again and again. He was patient, yet at the right time he spoke plainly. Jesus would bear with weakness while managing his time and drawing strength from the Father.

b.p: “We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak.” Our experience is a gift given to support others. But bearing isn’t carrying without limit; it is helping people grow wisely and with a method.
b.t: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.

h: Lord, I confess I’m impatient. Enlarge my heart and give me good ways to help her while still keeping up with my own work.
g: Impatience and cutting remarks let self-centredness rule. Training someone with patience and wisdom lets Jesus be glorified in the contact centre.
x: My new colleague may already be nervous and lacking confidence, and my own work and wellbeing matter too. A good method keeps both of us from being hurt.
n: Set a fixed time each day to answer her questions together, and compile a list of common questions for her. Explain to your manager how much time training takes, and ask for an adjusted workload or deadlines.

t: Asked to draw up a redundancy list
s: I manage a department in a manufacturing firm. Orders have collapsed, and within two weeks I must choose five of my twenty staff for redundancy. The list might include a young father who has just bought a flat, an older technician near retirement, and someone average but very conscientious. I can’t sleep.
j: Jesus never treated people as numbers; he calls each of his sheep by name. He faced hard moments, yet always with compassion. Jesus would carry the responsibility that was his while doing all he could to protect each person’s dignity.

b.p: “To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God”: justice means clear, fair criteria; mercy means caring for people’s circumstances along the way; humility means remembering I too must give account to God.
b.t: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

h: Lord, this decision is so heavy. Give me wisdom and compassion, so that I neither dodge my responsibility nor go numb, and so that I see the family behind every name.
g: Choosing by friendships or self-interest lets prejudice be king. Acting fairly, transparently and with compassion lets Jesus be glorified in a hard season.
x: Those made redundant and their families bear the heaviest blow, and those who remain will feel insecure. Prepare clear explanations and support in advance, so that those leaving are respected and those staying feel safe.
n: Check legal procedures and compensation with HR first, assess by clear job criteria and avoid personal preferences; propose alternatives such as reduced hours or redeployment. Tell each person yourself, one to one, help with references and support services, and pray for each one.

t: Must I mark down my friend?
s: I lead a team at a software company. In this year’s appraisals, my closest colleague on the team has clearly fallen behind and by our standards should be rated ‘needs improvement’. He has had a hard year at home and privately begged me to “go easy, or my bonus will drop a lot”. The rest of the team can see how he has performed.
j: Jesus loved his disciples but didn’t show favouritism because they were close; he corrected Peter directly. Jesus would assess fairly and then, privately and lovingly, walk with him to help him back on his feet.

b.p: “You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favouritism to the great”, but judge in righteousness. Favouring a friend looks like love but is unfair to others. Real love includes honest feedback and practical help.
b.t: You shall do no injustice in judgement. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favouritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbour in righteousness.

h: Lord, it pains me. Help me find the balance between justice and mercy, and give me words that are honest and kind.
g: Favouritism gives glory to friendship and face. Fair appraisal with real support lets Jesus be King in how the team is run.
x: My friend will be disappointed, and other hardworking colleagues may lose heart if things are unfair. An honest assessment with a concrete improvement plan cares for him and the team alike.
n: Rate him fairly by the standard, then meet privately. Affirm his worth first, then explain the basis of the rating. Agree specific goals and support together, and if home life is affecting work, help him find out about flexible arrangements or support the company offers.

t: I have to dismiss an employee
s: I run a small interior design firm. One employee has been through three improvement conversations but still submits drawings late and makes mistakes that annoy clients. A brother from church introduced him, and he is a kind man. I keep putting off the conversation, so others have to clear up after him, and morale is sinking.
j: Jesus loves people, and his love includes telling the truth. He told the rich young man what he lacked, watched him go away sad, and still loved him. Jesus would make a hard decision gently and clearly.

b.p: “The wounds of a friend are faithful.” A true friend dares to speak painful truth. Delaying is really about sparing myself; ending the arrangement honestly may help him find a better-suited place.
b.t: The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

h: Lord, I’m afraid of hurting him and of being misunderstood at church. Keep my motives pure, and give me the right moment and gentle words.
g: Endless delay lets my conflict-avoiding self rule. Handling it responsibly lets Jesus be glorified in how the firm is managed.
x: The employee and his family, the brother who introduced him, and colleagues who have been covering for him all need care. Give him enough time, fair compensation and a reference to preserve his dignity and the relationship.
n: Prepare documentation in line with employment law and company policy, taking professional advice if needed, and tell him the decision and reasons privately and kindly. Offer a reasonable transition and help with job-seeking, and explain to the brother who introduced him so there is no misunderstanding.

t: Accused of favouritism
s: I’m an area manager for a coffee chain. At a meeting one store manager said bluntly that I always give the best promotions and resources to a certain branch “because its manager was your junior at university”. I believe I allocate by performance, but now I’m not sure I’ve been completely fair.
j: When criticised, Jesus didn’t rush to defend himself, and he was willing to answer honest questions. He was free of prejudice, valuing tax collectors and Pharisees alike. Jesus would examine himself first, then respond openly.

b.p: Those who hold the faith of our Lord Jesus must not do so “with partiality”. Favouritism often creeps in unnoticed; this verse invites us to examine our standards honestly, not just defend ourselves.
b.t: My brothers, dont hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality.

h: Lord, search my heart and show me biases I haven’t noticed. Keep me from resenting the accusation, and help me listen humbly.
g: Defending myself and silencing the critic lets pride be king. Humble review and open criteria let Jesus be glorified.
x: The store manager took a risk in speaking up and needs protecting; the branch manager shouldn’t be labelled either. The whole team needs confidence in fairness.
n: Thank the store manager for her honesty and meet her privately to hear what she has seen. Review last year’s allocation data, publish the criteria, and invite all store managers to help shape the rules.

t: Two key team members at odds
s: I head a hospital rehabilitation department. Two senior therapists have been at odds for a long time over rotas and patient allocation. They don’t speak, pass everything through me, and are even recruiting newer staff to their sides. Patients are starting to feel the tension in the treatment rooms.
j: Among Jesus’ disciples were a tax collector and a Zealot. He brought very different people together and taught them to love one another. Jesus would be a peacemaker, starting the conversation rather than acting as a go-between.

b.p: Peacemaking isn’t pretending all is well; it is actively working for reconciliation. Leaders are responsible for a peaceful workplace, and such people “shall be called children of God”.
b.t: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

h: Lord, I want to run away from this conflict. Give me courage and wisdom, to take neither side and to work for reconciliation with love.
g: Settling for surface calm lets my trouble-avoiding self rule. Working bravely for peace lets Jesus be glorified in the team.
x: Both therapists may feel wronged; newer staff are caught in the middle; patients’ care suffers. Every side needs to be heard.
n: Speak to each therapist privately first and listen to their grievances and needs; then hold a three-way meeting to agree fair rules for rotas and allocation. Involve HR or a professional mediator if needed, and stop acting as the go-between.

t: An older technician who can’t keep up
s: I manage a printing works. We’ve brought in digital equipment, and a technician with twenty-five years’ service simply can’t learn the new system. He makes mistakes and slows the line. Younger staff are complaining, and the general manager has hinted that I should “let him leave of his own accord”. He is four years from retirement.
j: Jesus didn’t give up on people because they were weak. He spoke comfort to the discouraged and gave the weak time, while being honest about reality. Jesus would honour the technician’s years of service and look for a place that suits him.

b.p: This verse gives leaders careful guidance: admonish the disorderly, encourage the faint-hearted, support the weak, and “be patient towards all”. This technician isn’t disorderly; he needs support and patience.
b.t: We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient towards all.

h: Lord, help me see this man’s value and not only his speed. Give me creativity to find a path that works for him and for the team.
g: Pushing someone to resign lets efficiency and coldness be king. Respectful, wise arrangements let Jesus be glorified in the works.
x: The technician’s dignity and livelihood, the younger staff’s pressure and the company’s efficiency all need care. Don’t let him leave in humiliation.
n: Arrange one-to-one training and a longer learning period, or move him to a role that uses his experience, such as quality checks or training newcomers. Talk honestly with him. If changes are still needed, handle them lawfully and help him plan for retirement with dignity.

t: I keep losing my temper with my team
s: I’m a site manager for a construction company. With tight deadlines and bad weather, I shout at my team on site whenever they make a mistake, and I sometimes throw my hard hat down. Two young engineers recently resigned, and both said in their exit interviews that I was “too harsh”. I know I have a problem but can’t control it.
j: Jesus is “gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He knew righteous anger, but he never took out pressure on people; when his disciples failed, he still led them gently. Jesus would help me admit my fault first, then learn a new way to lead.

b.p: Be “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger”, because “the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God”. Shouting may speed things up for a moment, but it never builds a good team.
b.t: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesnt produce the righteousness of God.

h: Lord, I admit my anger has hurt people. In the moment before I explode, remind me to breathe and to listen before I speak.
g: Managing by anger lets my self-centred need for control be king. Learning to lead gently and firmly lets Jesus be glorified on site.
x: My team’s wellbeing and dignity, the stability of the team, and my own health and family are all affected. Apologising to those I’ve hurt is where repair begins.
n: Own up to your team and apologise, and set yourself a ‘pause’ routine, such as stepping away for five minutes and praying first. Ask a trusted colleague to hold you accountable. If your anger is hard to control, seek professional counselling.

t: Should I ask for a pay rise?
s: I’ve worked at a design studio for four years. My salary has never been reviewed, my workload has doubled, and I now train two juniors. I know the market rate is about a fifth higher, but talking about money feels grubby, as if a Christian should simply be content. My boss treats me reasonably well.
j: Jesus taught that “the labourer is worthy of his wages”; he didn’t think fair pay unspiritual, and he wasn’t bound by money. Jesus would make a reasonable request with peace and honesty, then leave the outcome with the Father.

b.p: Contentment doesn’t mean never discussing pay. Fair wages are affirmed by God. Raising it respectfully is taking responsibility for your work and being honest with your employer.
b.t: Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the labourer is worthy of his wages. Dont go from house to house.

h: Lord, help me discern: is this greed or a fair need? Let me go in with gratitude and peace, without resentment and without fear of a no.
g: Staying unhappy, silent and grumbling lets bitterness rule. Grateful, honest conversation lets Jesus be glorified in the pay discussion.
x: My relationship with my boss and the studio’s finances both need care. Don’t threaten to leave; use concrete contributions and market data so there is room on both sides.
n: Gather your specific contributions from the past year and market salary data, and book a proper meeting. Begin with thanks, then state your hopes. If the studio can’t adjust now, discuss alternatives such as flexible hours, training support or a timetable for review.

t: Headhunted just when we need me
s: I’m the first engineer at a start-up. A competitor is offering double my salary, and my family needs a bigger home. But we’re at a crucial funding stage, the founder trusts me completely, and if I leave now the product launch could slip.
j: Jesus wasn’t driven by gain or held hostage by guilt; everything he did flowed from the Father’s will. Jesus would face his needs honestly in prayer and honour the commitment in this partnership.

b.p: “Godliness with contentment is great gain” reminds us not to let money be the only consideration. It doesn’t forbid changing jobs; it grounds the decision in God’s guidance and integrity.
b.t: But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly cant carry anything out.

h: Lord, I’m drawn to this offer and pulled by responsibility. Quieten me so I can hear your voice, not just the numbers.
g: Looking only at money lets Mammon be king; staying only out of guilt lets others’ expectations be king. A decision made in prayer with peace lets Jesus be glorified.
x: The founder, the team and my family all have real needs. If I go, I should say so honestly and hand over well; if I stay, I can still talk openly about my needs.
n: Pray with your spouse and list the considerations, and talk frankly with the founder about your situation and hopes. If you decide to leave, give a full handover period, take no confidential material, and part on good terms.

t: My side job uses company resources
s: I’m a video editor at an advertising agency, and I take freelance jobs in the evenings to help with family finances. Lately there are more of them, and I’ve started replying to clients during work hours and using the agency’s licensed software and stock library for my own projects. No one seems to have noticed.
j: Jesus said no one can serve two masters. He was wholly faithful to what was entrusted to him and never used others’ resources for his own gain. Jesus would draw a clear line between the two jobs and be honest about his time and resources.

b.p: A side job isn’t necessarily wrong, but when money pulls the heart, the main job is neglected and company resources are used, we are trying to “serve two masters”. God wants our hearts to have one clear Lord.
b.t: No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cant serve both God and Mammon.

h: Lord, show me whether money is already leading my heart. Give me the honest courage to separate what should be kept apart.
g: Using work time and resources in secret gives glory to greed. Keeping clear boundaries lets Jesus be glorified in both jobs.
x: The agency’s interests, colleagues’ trust and freelance clients’ need for proper licences could all be affected. Correcting it early prevents greater harm later.
n: Stop freelance work during office hours, and buy your own software and licensed assets. Check the company’s policy on outside work and declare it to your manager if required. If freelancing affects your main job, honestly assess which to reduce.

t: A colleague’s high-return investment
s: I’m a civil servant with a steady income. A very enthusiastic colleague is urging me to invest in a cryptocurrency platform promising five per cent a month. He says he has already earned a car, and that bringing in more colleagues earns a bonus. I would love to save more so my children can study abroad one day.
j: Jesus saw into people’s hearts and wasn’t dazzled by surface gain. He taught people to store up treasure in heaven, not because money is unimportant but so that it doesn’t master the heart. Jesus would weigh this calmly and also care for this colleague.

b.p: “Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away.” Easy-sounding high returns usually hide high risks. God delights in diligent, steady saving that “makes it grow”.
b.t: Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away, but he who gathers by hand makes it grow.

h: Lord, I want my children to have a good future. Keep me from being driven by anxiety and greed, and give me clear discernment.
g: Chasing quick money lets greed be king. Managing money steadily lets Jesus be my family’s provider, and he receives the glory.
x: My colleague may already be at risk, and anyone I bring in could be hurt even more. I needn’t mock him; I can gently share my concerns.
n: Decline to invest and don’t recruit anyone else. Check the financial regulator’s warning list or consult a qualified financial adviser. Make a steady long-term savings plan for your children’s education and discuss it with your spouse.

t: A colleague asks to borrow money
s: I’m a mechanic at a car repair garage. A colleague says a family member is in hospital and he urgently needs thirty thousand, and he has asked me for a loan. He borrowed once before and took six months to repay. I do have the money, but it’s for my rent. He looks truly desperate.
j: Jesus was full of compassion for people’s needs; he fed the hungry and healed the sick. Yet his help was always wise, not driven by others’ emotions. Jesus would respond with love while keeping his responsibilities to his own household.

b.p: God urges us, “Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it.” But doing good should match our means and care for our own families, and lending is not the only way to help.
b.t: Dont withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it.

h: Lord, give me a compassionate heart and clear judgement. Show me how much and how to help, so I decide out of neither guilt nor coldness.
g: A cold refusal lets self-protection be king; lending regardless of my family lets someone else’s pressure be king. Responding with love and wisdom lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My colleague, his relative in hospital and my own family all need care. If a loan could damage the friendship, a gift within my means, with no expectation of return, may preserve it better.
n: Work out what you can afford. You might lend part of it or give a smaller gift, and agree clearly how it will be repaid. You could also help him find hospital assistance or an emergency fund at work, and pray for his family.

t: How to share a team bonus fairly
s: I manage the marketing team, and the company has given us a project bonus for me to divide. One senior colleague is very popular but contributed little this time; a newcomer quietly did the most but isn’t good at speaking up. If I divide by contribution, the senior colleague may be upset and the team mood could sour.
j: Jesus noticed the poor widow’s two small coins; he saw the giving others missed, and he wasn’t afraid of offending the well regarded. Jesus would divide fairly according to actual contribution and explain his reasons clearly.

b.p: In sharing the bonus, act not “through rivalry or through conceit”, and be “not just looking to his own things”: decide not for popularity or to avoid trouble, but out of genuine care for each colleague’s work.
b.t: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

h: Lord, show me everyone’s real contribution, give me courage to decide fairly, and give me gentle words to explain.
g: Dividing unfairly to dodge conflict lets favour and avoidance be king. Fair, transparent sharing lets Jesus be glorified in the team.
x: The newcomer who worked quietly needs to be seen; the senior colleague needs respect, not humiliation. Clear criteria and private conversations can care for both.
n: Set clear criteria beforehand (hours, results, roles) and divide accordingly. Speak to each person privately: affirm the senior colleague’s other strengths, and thank the newcomer specifically for the work done.

t: I earn far less than my friends
s: I’m a social worker at a welfare charity, earning half what my university friends make in tech. At reunions they talk about buying homes and travelling abroad, and I just smile along. Afterwards I start doubting my choices and wonder if I should switch careers to earn more.
j: Jesus said the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, yet he wasn’t ashamed; he knew the Father’s mission was worth more than wealth, and he never dismissed real needs. Jesus would lead me out of the pain of comparison back to the Father, to find my true worth.

b.p: Paul’s contentment was something he had “learnt”, not something he was born with. Contentment isn’t giving up hope; it is trusting God in plenty and in need, so that comparison doesn’t steal our joy.
b.t: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learnt in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learnt the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.

h: Lord, I confess comparison has robbed me of joy. Show me again the meaning of your call on my life, and help me face our real financial needs honestly.
g: A choice driven by comparison lets the world’s standards be king. Faithful contentment, or a prayerful change of path, can both let Jesus be glorified.
x: My family’s finances, the clients I serve and my own wellbeing all need care. Changing career isn’t a sin, but don’t rush into it out of comparison alone.
n: Review your real financial needs with your family and set a budget. Spend time in prayer and talk to a trusted spiritual mentor or careers adviser. If the financial pressure is real, consider further study or development within your field.

t: Long-term overwork, warning lights on
s: I’m an analyst at an investment bank. For six months I’ve worked fourteen-hour days and am often called in at weekends. Recently I’ve had palpitations and hair loss, and my health check flagged several results in red. My manager says, “Just get through these two years,” and I don’t want to disappoint my family.
j: At the busiest point of his ministry, Jesus still took his disciples to a quiet place to rest, and he invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest. Jesus would take the body’s warnings seriously and not mistake overwork for faithfulness.

b.p: Jesus’ invitation is not ‘hold on a bit longer’ but “Come to me”. His yoke is easy. When our yoke is so heavy it crushes our body, we must ask: is this really the burden the Lord has given?
b.t: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

h: Lord, I’m so tired. Help me stop and face my body and soul honestly, and help me believe that you love me not because of how much I do.
g: Trading health for achievement lets the idol of success be king. Finding rest in the Lord and caring for my body lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My body and my family are the first to be hurt, and long-term overwork also affects the quality of work and judgement. Caring for myself is responsible love.
n: See a doctor soon and follow medical advice, and talk honestly with your family. Discuss your workload with your manager and set basic limits for rest. If nothing changes, consider a different role or job, and seek help from someone you trust or a professional.

t: Weekend overtime again
s: I’m an engineer at a building consultancy. Almost every Friday just before home time my manager hands me work “needed Monday morning”, so I often work weekends. I’ve cancelled my children’s matches and family trips again and again. If I say no, I fear a poor appraisal.
j: Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man”; he valued people above rules and performance. He worked when needed, but didn’t let work swallow the rhythm of life. Jesus would handle this honestly and protect his family.

b.p: Rest is God’s gift to people, not a luxury on top of work. Occasional overtime is understandable, but when rest and family time are taken away for long, our rhythm needs re-examining.
b.t: He said to them, The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

h: Lord, help me remember that rest is your grace to me. Give me courage to talk with my manager, and help me keep my promises to my family.
g: Always saying yes lets my fearful self be king. Wisely setting boundaries lets Jesus be glorified in how I use my time.
x: My children’s and spouse’s trust is draining away, and colleagues may face the same. Approach your manager with solutions in mind, protecting the relationship.
n: Midweek, check next week’s priorities and ask your manager to assign work earlier. Explain your family commitments and agree together what counts as urgent. When overtime is genuinely needed, tell your family in advance and make up the time with them afterwards.

t: Rostered on every Sunday
s: I’m front-of-house manager at a restaurant. Weekends are our busiest time, and the owner has put me on full shifts every Sunday. I haven’t been to Sunday worship or my small group for three months, and my faith feels drier and drier. Changing jobs isn’t easy, and I’m torn.
j: Jesus went to the synagogue as was his custom, valuing worship with God’s people; he also healed on the Sabbath, showing that its spirit is love and mercy. Jesus would look for a sustainable rhythm of worship without falling into legalism or guilt.

b.p: “Not forsaking our own assembling together” is about a shared life of caring for and encouraging one another. What matters is not a particular time slot but not cutting ourselves off from the community of faith.
b.t: Lets consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

h: Lord, I miss worshipping with my brothers and sisters. Please open a way, and let me know your presence even at work.
g: Giving up gathering for good may let work be king. Actively finding ways to keep worshipping lets Jesus be glorified in my life.
x: My spiritual life needs the support of community; the owner and colleagues also have rota pressures. Honest conversation and understanding are better than silent resentment.
n: Explain your faith needs to the owner and ask for at least one or two Sundays off each month, or swap shifts with colleagues. Meanwhile join a midweek or Saturday gathering or small group, and find a spiritual companion to pray with regularly.

t: Work anxiety keeps me awake
s: I run a tutoring centre. It’s enrolment season and numbers are down by a third on last year. Every night as soon as I lie down I start working through the figures; at three in the morning I’m still answering messages, and then I force myself to teach. I haven’t slept well for a month.
j: The disciples panicked in the storm, but Jesus slept in the stern, because he trusted the Father completely. He did care about them; he simply had peace in the storm. Jesus would hand tomorrow’s worries to the Father and sleep in peace.

b.p: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil.” Effort isn’t sin, but if we believe everything depends on us we lose our sleep. “He gives sleep to his loved ones” as the fruit of trust.
b.t: It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

h: Lord, tonight I hand the enrolment figures to you. Quieten my heart, and help me believe you care even more than I do about this centre and its pupils.
g: Lying awake with worry lets the self that says ‘it all depends on me’ be king. Handing over the burden lets Jesus be glorified even in my sleep.
x: My health, my family, even my teachers and pupils are affected by my anxiety. Resting well is part of my responsibility to them.
n: Turn off work messages an hour before bed, write down tomorrow’s tasks, then commit them to God in prayer. Share the enrolment work with your team. If sleeplessness persists, see a doctor or other professional.

t: Burnt out and empty
s: I’ve been a project manager at a non-profit for eight years. I used to be passionate; now I don’t want to get up in the morning, emails make me irritable, and I feel numb towards colleagues and the people we serve. I feel I’m not a good Christian any more, yet I can’t say what is wrong.
j: After a mighty work of God, Elijah collapsed and asked to die. God didn’t rebuke him; he let him sleep and eat first, then spoke to him gently. Jesus also understands human weakness. He would care for a weary body and soul first, rather than demand more spirituality.

b.p: God’s word to his exhausted servant was “Arise and eat”, adding “the journey is too great for you.” Rest and recovery are God’s will, not a mark of failure.
b.t: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. The LORDs angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”

h: Lord, I feel empty. Please don’t just give me strength to keep going; first let me rest in you and be given new life.
g: Struggling on and pretending all is well lets ‘I must perform’ be king. Facing burnout honestly and accepting recovery lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wellbeing needs care most of all, and long-term burnout also affects the team and those we serve. Telling people around me is the start of preventing greater harm.
n: Talk with your manager about reducing your load or taking leave. Keep regular hours, exercise, and rediscover things that bring you joy. Talk with a trusted spiritual mentor, and if low mood persists, seek professional counselling or see a doctor.

t: My child says I’m never home
s: I’m in export sales, travel constantly, and take client calls even when I’m home. Last week my seven-year-old daughter drew a family picture without me in it. “Because you’re never here,” she said. It shook me, but the company is opening new markets and my manager expects me to lead the push.
j: When Martha was flustered, Jesus gently reminded her that “one thing is needed”; he also took little children in his arms and blessed them. Jesus would help me reorder my priorities so that those I love can feel my presence.

b.p: Martha was doing good things but was filled with “many things”. Jesus wasn’t dismissing work; he was helping us see “the good part”. Our relationship with God and family is something that must not be taken away.
b.t: Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

h: Lord, help me hear my daughter’s heart and stop using busyness as an excuse. Show me what the one needed thing is in this season.
g: Letting targets fill my life lets the idol of work be king. Reordering priorities lets Jesus be glorified in my home.
x: My daughter and spouse are most affected, and my manager and clients have needs too. People matter more than tasks; family is not a relationship that can wait for ‘later’.
n: Agree regular family time with your spouse and children, such as no calls at dinner and half a day together at weekends. Explain your family needs to your manager and discuss travel frequency or sharing the load. Today, draw a new family picture with your daughter, with you in it.

t: Messages that never stop
s: I’m a product manager at a tech company. After hours, messages from my manager and colleagues never stop; at eleven at night someone tags me in the group chat, and weekends are the same. If I don’t reply I look irresponsible; if I do, I’m in work mode all night. My family says I’m there in body but not in mind.
j: Jesus’ life held both work and withdrawal. He rose before dawn to pray in a solitary place and was not endlessly pulled along by the crowds’ demands. Jesus would set fitting boundaries so that work had a beginning and an end.

b.p: “You shall labour six days”, and then comes “the seventh day”. In God’s rhythm work has limits, and those limits include even “your male servant” and “your female servant”: God’s protection of people.
b.t: You shall labour six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates.

h: Lord, keep me from being ruled by notification sounds. Give me courage to set boundaries, and help me believe the world won’t stop if I reply a little later.
g: Always being on call lets work and anxiety be king. Keeping a boundary for rest lets Jesus be King of my time.
x: My family needs me present, and the team needs clear ways of communicating. Agreeing rules with my manager benefits us both.
n: Agree with your manager and team what counts as urgent, with a phone call only for real emergencies. Mute group notifications after hours and check once at a set time; at home, leave your phone outside the living room and give your family your attention.

t: Perfectionism and fear of mistakes
s: I’m an associate at a law firm. I revise every pleading into the small hours, checking every comma, terrified the partner will find an error. As a result I often miss deadlines, the partner says I’m “too slow”, and I feel even more anxious, as if I’ll never be good enough.
j: Peter denied the Lord three times, yet Jesus welcomed him back and restored his calling. Jesus’ love isn’t built on performance. He would remind me that my worth comes from the Father’s love, not from making no mistakes.

b.p: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Perfectionism often tries to prove our worth by ourselves; God invites us to rest in his grace.
b.t: He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.

h: Lord, I’m so afraid of not being good enough. Help me relax in your grace, accept my limits, and find peace in my work because of you.
g: Chasing zero errors lets the self that must be perfect be king. Doing my best in grace and accepting imperfection lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wellbeing, my family, and the colleagues and clients waiting for documents are all affected. Delivering good-enough work on time is also a way of loving the team.
n: Set a reasonable completion time and a checklist for each task, and submit when time is up. Ask the partner to clarify the quality standard. If anxiety seriously affects your life, seek help from someone you trust or a professional.

t: Colleagues mock my faith
s: I’m a video editor at a TV station. Since colleagues learnt I’m a Christian, they often joke at lunch: “Aren’t you supposed to love people? Then do my overtime,” or “Does believing in Jesus mean you can’t have any fun?” Sometimes they swear in front of me on purpose to see how I react.
j: When Jesus was mocked he sometimes stayed silent and sometimes asked a question that made people think. He didn’t rush to defend himself, yet he remained gentle and steady. Jesus would answer with humour and kindness, letting his life speak rather than arguing.

b.p: First “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts”, then answer “with humility and fear”. When mocked, there is no need to hit back or to hide our faith; a good way of life is the strongest answer.
b.t: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear, having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.

h: Lord, keep me from being provoked by mockery and from being ashamed of you. Give me kind words and a sense of humour, so that colleagues see your love.
g: Angry retorts let pride be king; hiding my faith lets fear be king. Living out faith gently and openly lets Jesus be glorified.
x: Colleagues who joke may be curious about faith or misunderstand it, and I also deserve respect. Gently stating boundaries keeps the relationship and protects me.
n: Take the jokes lightly, and if needed tell someone privately and gently that certain remarks make you uncomfortable. Keep showing honesty and kindness at work. When a colleague genuinely wants to know, find time to share your story of faith.

t: Pressed to drink at client dinners
s: I’m a sales manager at a trading company and often host clients for dinner. Drinking culture is strong: clients say, “Not drinking means you don’t respect us,” and my boss hints that tonight decides the order. Last time I drank until I blacked out and deeply regretted it, but I’m afraid that refusing will lose the deal.
j: Jesus celebrated at the wedding in Cana and ate with tax collectors and sinners; he was not aloof. Yet he never lost his clarity or his boundaries. Jesus would join in the occasion while keeping a life filled with the Spirit.

b.p: Scripture forbids being “drunken with wine, in which is dissipation”, losing self-control. We may have freedom about drinking, but alcohol must not master us; people “filled with the Spirit” know how to stay clear-headed.
b.t: Dont be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.

h: Lord, be with me at the dinner table. Give me wise words and a steady heart, so that I am not afraid of offending people and do not lose self-control.
g: Drinking until I lose control lets face and sales be king. Taking part with restraint and keeping boundaries lets Jesus be glorified at business dinners.
