x: My health, my family’s worries and the client’s face all need care. A respectful refusal protects relationships better than a blunt one.
n: Set your limit beforehand, or toast with tea, explaining reasons of health and family. Build client relationships through genuine care, expertise and service. Talk with your boss too, so he understands your principles.

t: Company rituals at the shrine
s: I work in administration at a traditional manufacturing company. On the first and fifteenth of each lunar month and at the Hungry Ghost Festival, the whole company makes offerings, and my boss has put me in charge of preparing them and leading the incense. I don’t want him to think I’m uncooperative, nor to go against my faith. It makes me anxious every time.
j: Daniel served faithfully in Babylon yet never compromised in worship, and he made his request respectfully. Jesus respected and served people all his life, but worshipped only the Father. Jesus would help in other ways without compromising faith.

b.p: “Whatever you do, do all to the glory of God”, and “give no occasion for stumbling”. We do not take part in idol worship, but with respect and humility we can keep our refusal from becoming an offence.
b.t: Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, to Greeks, or to the assembly of God.

h: Lord, give me courage to keep faith and gentle words to explain to my boss. Let my refusal carry respect, not opposition.
g: Joining in to please others lets human power be king; refusing harshly lets self-righteousness be king. Holding to faith gently and firmly lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My boss and colleagues have their own traditions and beliefs, and I have my conscience. Respectful conversation can prevent a rupture in relationships.
n: Explain your faith privately to your boss: you cannot offer incense or lead the ritual, but you will gladly take on other administrative work instead. Work even more diligently day by day so he sees your loyalty, and pray blessing on him and your colleagues.

t: A grieving colleague asks about my faith
s: I handle claims at an insurance company. A colleague’s father died suddenly, and in the pantry, red-eyed, she asked me, “Where do you Christians believe people go when they die?” Others in the office could hear. I long to comfort her but I’m afraid of saying the wrong thing or seeming to take advantage to evangelise.
j: Jesus wept at Lazarus’ tomb. He grieved with those who grieved before he spoke of resurrection hope. He never exploited pain; he truly stayed alongside. Jesus would offer comfort first, and share hope when the time was right.

b.p: “Walk in wisdom towards those who are outside”, and let your speech “always be with grace”. When answering questions of faith, timing and manner matter as much as content: be present first, then share hope in simple, gentle words.
b.t: Walk in wisdom towards those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

h: Lord, give me fitting words. Let me comfort her first, and when she is ready, share the resurrection hope you give.
g: Seizing the moment to lecture may let ‘I must evangelise successfully’ be king. Gentle presence and timely sharing let Jesus’ love be glorified.
x: My colleague is at her most fragile; her need matters more than my need to explain. Respect her family’s beliefs too, and never criticise her relatives.
n: Offer your condolences and invite her somewhere quiet to talk. Share briefly the hope you hold, and ask whether she would like to know more. Keep caring afterwards, send a card, and remember her in prayer.

t: A workplace course with religious rituals
s: I work in HR at a multinational. For staff wellbeing the company has booked a series of ‘mindfulness meditation’ sessions, and the facilitator includes religious rituals such as prayers to a deity and chanting mantras. My manager wants everyone to attend, and I’m organising it.
j: Daniel excelled in a foreign court yet kept clear boundaries in his faith. Jesus cares for body and mind, and worships the Father alone. Jesus would support the company’s good intention while wisely proposing changes that don’t violate faith.

b.p: Daniel “purposed in his heart” not to defile himself, yet he “requested” rather than resisted. He offered an alternative; holding to principle and respecting authority can go together.
b.t: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the kings delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

h: Lord, help me discern what is simply relaxation and health and what is a religious ritual I cannot join. Give me wisdom to make a fitting suggestion.
g: Joining in without discernment lets pleasing people be king; refusing angrily lets self-righteousness be king. A wise adjustment lets Jesus be glorified at work.
x: The company’s good intentions, colleagues of other faiths and my own conscience all need care. Proposing changes out of respect for every employee’s beliefs benefits everyone.
n: Suggest to your manager that the sessions be reshaped as relaxation or stress management without religious rituals, explaining that this better respects colleagues of all faiths. If the rituals remain, ask to sit out that part yourself.

t: Laughed at for praying before meals
s: I’m a graduate who has just joined a tech company, and I usually bow my head to pray before eating. At a team dinner my manager saw and laughed, “This isn’t church,” and the whole table laughed. Since then I’ve felt embarrassed to pray, and also feel I’ve betrayed my faith.
j: Jesus gave thanks for the five loaves and two fish in front of the crowd; his thanks were natural and sincere. He didn’t pray to show off, nor hide out of fear. Jesus would keep praying in a peaceful, unshowy way and look on those who laughed without judgement.

b.p: Letting our light shine is about “good works”, so that people “glorify your Father who is in heaven”. Prayer isn’t a performance; it can be quiet and simple. True light is also found in everyday words and deeds.
b.t: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

h: Lord, take away my shame and fear. Help me thank you naturally, and make my life a light my colleagues can see.
g: Hiding out of fear lets fear be king; making a show lets self be king. Keeping faith naturally and humbly lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My manager and colleagues may simply not understand, and I also need freedom to practise my faith. Responding lightly keeps it from becoming a confrontation.
n: Keep saying a short silent grace, neither drawing attention nor hiding. You could answer lightly, “Just grateful for the food.” Day by day, let your faith be seen through a good work ethic and kindness to others.

t: “You Christians are all fake”
s: I work at an advertising agency. A manager in our department calls himself a Christian but often lies, takes credit and is harsh with staff. When colleagues found out I’m a Christian too, one said coldly, “You Christians are all the same: fake.” I want to explain, but I also think that manager really is behaving badly.
j: Jesus sternly rebuked hypocritical religious leaders and never defended hypocrisy; yet he called his disciples to bear witness by loving one another. Jesus would admit the problem and point with his life to the true gospel.

b.p: People recognise disciples not by argument but by “love for one another”. We can’t defend others’ behaviour, but with love and authenticity we can let people see what Christ is like.
b.t: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.

h: Lord, keep me from rushing to defend Christians; help me humbly admit our imperfection. Let my life become a chance for colleagues to know you afresh.
g: Rushing to distance myself or to defend may let my reputation be king. Humble admission and living out love let Jesus be glorified.
x: Colleagues may have been hurt by that manager, and he too needs prayer and honest reminders. Don’t criticise him behind his back, and don’t ignore colleagues’ feelings.
n: Acknowledge how your colleague feels: “I understand. Christians fail too.” Show care in action for those who have been hurt. If there is an opportunity, speak to that manager privately in love, and keep praying for him.

t: A secure job or my dream?
s: I’ve been a bank cashier for eight years. The job is secure with good benefits, but every day I feel I’m just counting notes. I’ve always loved baking; I take weekend classes and my teacher says I have real talent. My family think I’m mad to give up a job for life to make bread.
j: Jesus began his public ministry at about thirty, and every step sought the Father’s will rather than his own impulses or others’ expectations. Jesus would wait patiently for the Father’s time, and step out bravely when it came.

b.p: We may plan our course, but the Lord directs our steps. This verse encourages careful planning while staying open for God to adjust our direction along the way.
b.t: A mans heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.

h: Lord, help me discern: is this a calling you have placed in my heart, or a wish to escape? Let me hear your voice in prayer.
g: Quitting on impulse may let ‘I want freedom’ be king; staying only for security may let fear be king. Deciding in prayer and wisdom lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My family’s worries are real, and financial and household needs must be considered. Decide together with them, not alone.
n: Test it first without resigning: take weekend orders and sell at markets to build experience and customers. Set a financial reserve and timetable, pray and talk it through with your family and a spiritual mentor, and then decide whether to make the change.

t: Leaving to start a business
s: I’m a senior engineer at a tech company, and two friends and I want to build an education app together. I’ve saved a year’s living costs, but my wife is worried: the children are young and the mortgage is heavy. My friends are urging me to resign next month: “Opportunities don’t wait.”
j: Jesus taught that before building a tower we should first sit down and count the cost. He didn’t encourage blind risk, nor dismiss acts of faith. Jesus would plan in faith and respect his family’s feelings.

b.p: To “first sit down and count the cost” is wisdom within faith. Starting a business needs courage, and also an honest look at funds, time and what the family can bear; faith and planning are not opposites.
b.t: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesnt first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?

h: Lord, quieten me in both my excitement and my fear. Make my wife and me of one mind as we seek your guidance together.
g: Listening only to my friends’ urging lets impulse be king; giving up only out of fear lets fear be king. Deciding in prayer, united with my family, lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wife and children are most directly affected, and my partners’ expectations need an honest answer. Being of one mind as a couple matters more than racing the clock.
n: With your wife, set financial limits and a timetable, such as a one-year trial and a return to employment if funds run out. Seek advice from Christians who have started businesses or from a consultant, and if needed begin part-time until conditions are right.

t: A posting abroad my family opposes
s: I’m a manager at a multinational, and the company wants to send me to our factory in Vietnam for three years, with an attractive promotion and pay rise. My wife has a secure teaching post in Taiwan, and our child has just started secondary school and doesn’t want to leave friends. I must answer within two weeks.
j: Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before choosing his disciples; on the cross he still entrusted his mother to a disciple’s care. Jesus would put his family at the centre of the decision, not just the career opportunity.

b.p: “In a multitude of counsellors they are established.” Don’t make a major career decision alone; consult your spouse, family and spiritual mentors, so that everyone is heard.
b.t: Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counsellors they are established.

h: Lord, make our family one in heart, and don’t let this opportunity become a rift between us. Help us seek your will together in prayer.
g: Dragging my family along for promotion lets career be king. Deciding together as a family, whether we go or stay, lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wife’s work, my child’s adjustment and our marriage would all be affected. Family objections aren’t obstacles but reminders from God.
n: Sit down as a family and let everyone share their worries and hopes. Ask the company about flexible options such as a shorter posting or family travel allowances. Pray together, talk to families with experience of postings abroad, and then decide together.

t: Suddenly made redundant
s: I’ve been an editor at a media company for twelve years. In a big digital restructuring I was suddenly told I must leave in a month. I’m forty-eight, afraid I won’t find work, and deeply ashamed. I don’t know how to tell my family or my friends at church.
j: Jesus was rejected by people and deserted by his disciples, yet he knew the Father still reigned; he didn’t let human opinion define him. Jesus would walk with those who have lost, and still see the Father’s hand in the dark.

b.p: “All things work together for good” doesn’t mean redundancy is good, but that God can work in the hardest places “for those who love God”. Losing a job does not define our worth.
b.t: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.

h: Lord, I’m frightened and ashamed. Hold me, and remind me that my worth is in you. Open a way for me, and help me trust you while I wait.
g: Being bound by shame and anxiety lets the world’s standards be king. Trusting God in loss lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My family will worry too, and friends at church want to help. Speaking up isn’t weakness; it gives love a chance to flow.
n: First check your redundancy pay and rights, taking professional advice if needed. Share honestly with your family and set a household budget together. Update your CV, contact your network and join a career transition course; find someone you trust to walk with you, and seek counselling if needed.

t: Retired and lost my role
s: I’ve just retired as head teacher of a secondary school after thirty-five years in education. Now I’m at home every day and don’t know what to do. Former colleagues rarely get in touch, and my wife says I’ve become irritable. I often feel useless.
j: Jesus’ worth lay not in a position but in his relationship with the Father; he never needed a title to prove himself. Jesus would help me see that life’s seasons change, but God’s call and love never do.

b.p: The righteous “will still produce fruit in old age”. Retirement isn’t the end but a new season; God can still use our experience, wisdom and time to bear new fruit.
b.t: They will still produce fruit in old age. They will be full of sap and green.

h: Lord, help me understand that my worth isn’t in a position but in you. Guide me in this new season to serve you and bless others.
g: Wallowing in loss lets my former identity be king. Being used by God afresh in a new season lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My wife needs my companionship and understanding, and my children and grandchildren may long for more time with me. A new season is also a chance to mend and deepen relationships.
n: Plan a new rhythm of life with your wife and take up new interests. Serve at church, perhaps helping children with homework, leading a Bible study or mentoring young teachers. If low mood lasts, seek help from someone you trust or a professional.

t: Unclear calling: full-time ministry?
s: I’m an engineer at a tech company and very involved in serving at church. After several recent sermons I’ve wondered whether I should resign, go to seminary and serve full-time. But I also love my job and feel I have influence at work. I’m confused and don’t know what God wants of me.
j: Jesus called some to leave their nets and follow him, and sent a man he had healed back home to tell his family. His callings differ, but at heart they are all to follow him. Jesus would help me see that God can be served wholeheartedly anywhere.

b.p: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus.” Full-time ministry isn’t the only way to serve; working in the Lord’s name in the marketplace is also God’s calling. What matters is whether my life is in his hands.
b.t: Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

h: Lord, help me recognise your voice, and not be driven by passing emotion or pressure. Make clear to me where you want me to serve you.
g: Changing path just to seem more spiritual may let my image be king. Responding faithfully to your call in prayer, wherever it leads, lets Jesus be glorified.
x: My family, my church and colleagues at work will all be affected. This decision needs to be sought together with family and spiritual mentors.
n: Meet regularly with a pastor or spiritual mentor and pray with your family. Consider a part-time seminary course or short-term ministry first, and watch for God’s leading and inner peace rather than deciding in haste.

t: Promotion or staying technical?
s: I’m a senior software engineer, and the company wants to promote me to head of department, with more pay and status. But what I really love is coding, I’m not good at people management, and I worry that doing it badly would hurt the team. Family and colleagues all say, “It’s a rare chance; you must take it.”
j: When the crowds wanted to make Jesus king by force, he withdrew to the mountain and didn’t stray from the mission the Father gave him; he used his time and abilities according to the Father’s will. Jesus would help me see that gifts differ and each has its place.

b.p: We have “gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us”. Promotion isn’t necessarily God’s leading; knowing our gifts helps us serve where we can best glorify God and bless others.
b.t: having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, lets prophesy according to the proportion of our faith.

h: Lord, help me know my gifts and not be swayed by status or others’ expectations. Let me choose the place where you will be most glorified.
g: Accepting just for the title may let status be king; refusing out of fear may let fear be king. Choosing by gifting and calling lets Jesus be glorified.
x: The team needs a good leader, and my family will be affected too. Facing my gifts honestly is taking responsibility for the team.
n: Talk honestly with your manager about your considerations and ask whether there is a technical specialist track. You could first try leading a project to see whether managing people suits you, and pray with your family and a spiritual mentor.
